pages.translation:
After a hundred and one *yojanas*, he touched his crown and returned; with a single thought, he saw the Samantabhadra master.
Majestic, he is present on the red lotus seat;
Clearly, he is the white elephant child.
When the wisdom and compassion of the sand-kalpas are full,
When the vows and practices of the minute particles are perfect,
The Buddha's ocean of virtue is proclaimed again;
I worry to see the waves churning and vast. <gloss>Foguo Bai</gloss>

Beating the drum and playing the *pipa* <note>a four-stringed plucked lute</note>, he returns to his own assembly.
The wooden boy can clap his hands; the stone woman knows how to boil tea.
Clouds scatter, the moon appears at the edge of the sky; spring comes, flowers bloom on the trees.
Sudhana has visited everywhere; the black beans have not yet sprouted. <gloss>Yanqing Zhong</gloss>

<margin>Added sequel</margin> Sudhana traveled through one hundred and ten cities, visiting fifty-three good teachers. Finally, he arrived in front of the Vairochana Tower. The previous day was the place where one dwells in the emptiness, the signless, and the effortless <note>terms for the realization of non-attachment</note>. He saw the tower gate closed. Sudhana, for a moment, gathered his thoughts and said, "With great compassion, I pray that the tower gate opens and lets me enter." Maitreya, leading his retinue, arrived before Sudhana. With a snap of his fingers, the tower gate opened. Sudhana entered. Once inside, the gate closed again. He saw hundreds of thousands of billions of towers; in each tower, there was a Maitreya leading a retinue, and a Sudhana standing face to face before them. Maitreya snapped his fingers again and said, "Good man, arise. The nature of Dharma is like this."

A Verse says:

The wondrous intention of the child is collected at the very end.
Sudhana stops his southern journey here.
Suddenly he enters the Vairochana Treasury;
He regrets having gone to other mountains to see monks. <gloss>Zhang Wujin</gloss>

On the lone peak of Mount Miaofeng, there is no teacher.
Traveling to one hundred and ten cities was a waste for Sudhana.
If the tower were revealed by a snap of the fingers,
Clearly, one has eyes but has never opened them. <gloss>Huotian Ti</gloss>

Fifty-three people, strung on a single thread.
Though the child is small, his courage is like the sky.
Vast is the misty water, without number;
Buying the scenery costs no money at all. <gloss>Beijian Jian</gloss>

<summary>The page concludes Sudhana's journey at the Vairochana Tower, illustrating the realization of the non-dual, infinite nature of reality through Maitreya's guidance.</summary>
<keywords>Sudhana, Maitreya, Vairochana Tower, Non-duality, Chan realization</keywords>

...water, until today shining long in the slanting evening sun. <gloss>Guyun Quan</gloss>
Three inches from the hook, a shackle; one oar, and hundreds of thousands of pores feel a cold chill. Although both hands personally entrust it, it requires that fellow to nod his head himself. <gloss>Wujin Pai</gloss>
Jiashan in those years misused his mind. Greedy for the scented bait, he was captured by him. Nodding three times without a word; the water is wide, the mountains are distant, the resentment grows deeper. <gloss>Zheweng Yan</gloss>
With no place the size of an awl to contain his body, he instead drifts in a lone boat, occupying the crucial ferry. Not only did Jiashan suffer the poisonous hand, until today he has tricked to death a boatload of people. <gloss>Xiaoweng Kan</gloss>
Matching words to respond to the boatman is just like digging in the ground to seek the blue sky. Even if the oar were to thoroughly illuminate, it is still a leaky boat in Huating. <gloss>Sutai Bian</gloss>
No appearance and no flaw, then surrender. It is only because he lightly believed the wise wandering monk. If he had not arrived at Huating, what could the iron-cast boat oar do to you? <gloss>Nansou Jian</gloss>
In the depths of the Zhu River, a flat boat drifts. The clever wandering monk holds the straight hook. One oar to the mouth empties the universe. The distant mountains are layered, and the water is serene. <gloss>Gelu Tan</gloss>
In the laughter, he abandoned the Bamboo Grove Temple, thinking that Huating had much to offer. Exhausting life under the oar; thinking carefully, success and failure are just like Xiao He <note>a reference to the Han dynasty figure, implying fickle fortunes</note>. <gloss>Mozong Ben</gloss>
More than thirty years at Yaoshan, how could the life-activities of the ghost family be transmitted? At that time, if you had not obtained old Jiashan, you would just have to be patient and pole a broken boat. <gloss>Qingxi Che</gloss>

<column-break/>

Chuanzi instructed Jiashan, "From here on, you must go to a place where you hide your body and leave no traces. In the place where there are no traces, do not hide your body. I spent twenty years at Yaoshan only to clarify this matter. Now that you have obtained it, later do not reside in cities or crowded villages. Just go into the deep mountains and take a mattock <note>a digging tool, symbolizing a reclusive life of labor</note>..."

<summary>Further poetic reflections on the transmission between Chuanzi and Jiashan, followed by Chuanzi's final instructions to his successor.</summary>
<keywords>Transmission, Hiding traces, Yaoshan, Huating, Chan practice</keywords>

pages.translation:
# Deshan

<meta>The text discusses the encounter between the monk Luopu, his master Linji, and the master Deshan.</meta>

Luopu followed the instructions and asked. The master immediately struck. Luopu caught the staff and gave it a push. The master then returned to the abbot's quarters. Luopu returned and reported this to Linji. Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow. However, do you recognize Deshan?" Luopu hesitated, and Linji struck him.
<gloss>Added note</gloss>
The Xiongnu warrior prides himself on his skills, thinking he surpasses others. The young general goes to give orders. When he actually reaches the enemy, he wins a small battle, but upon returning, he cannot save his whole body <note>a metaphor for losing one's essence through arrogance</note>.
<gloss>Haiyin Xin</gloss>
<gloss>Fojian Qin</gloss>
Like a parrot in a golden cage, its back is like red jade, a green-clad servant. Although it has learned human speech, when you ask it something, it actually knows nothing at all.

<column-break/>

Deshan had a monk come to pay respects, and he shut the door. The monk knocked on the door. The master asked, "Who is it?" He replied, "A lion." The master opened the door. The monk circled in and bowed. The master jumped on his head and rode him, saying, "You animal, where have you been for so long?"
Verse:
<gloss>Added note</gloss>
Seeing a rabbit, one releases the hawk; by means of the false, one strikes the true. Before your feet have crossed the threshold, you must awaken suddenly.
<gloss>Mu'an Yong</gloss>
Deshan ascended the hall and said, "The great assembly knows it all. Even if the Buddhas of the three periods had their mouths hung on the wall, there would still be one person laughing loudly. If you recognize this person, your studies are complete."
<gloss>Or written as the secret words of Yuanming</gloss>
Touzi Qingyun said: Even so, the great companions of Deshan have hidden everything. The moon in the Chu sky still contains the stars of the Han land. He composed a verse:
The two blind men enter the dark, the road is rugged. The sun sets, the reeds provide a moment's rest. How can it compare to the stone man sleeping at midnight, avoiding the need for the emperor to guard the forest retreat? You must know that the blossoming of flowers is not related to the wood. When the legless one walks, he has already touched the path. Yesterday the wind rose on the Chang'an road; originally it was a map of the Kunlun frontier. I hold the throat, the wind grinds the clouds, the water is cold, the sky is autumn. Do not say the colorful scales have no flavor; he fished out the moon of the Canglang with one cast.
<note>Tiandong Jue</note>

<summary>This page presents dialogues regarding Deshan's aggressive teaching methods and metaphors for enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Deshan, Linji, Chan Buddhism, Verse, Study, Touzi Qing</keywords>

**Recorded Sayings of the Ancestral Masters**
Eighth generation after the Sixth Patriarch; seventh generation after Nanyang [Huizhong].

Chan Master Shouchu of Dongshan in Xiangzhou, a dharma heir of Yunmen. 
When he first visited Yunmen, the master asked, "Where did you just come from?"
The master replied, "Xixia."
[Yunmen] asked, "Where were you during the summer?"
The master replied, "Hunan."
[Yunmen] asked, "When did you leave Hunan?"
The master replied, "In the autumn."
[Yunmen] said, "I give you thirty blows."

The master asked, "What was my fault?"
[Yunmen] replied, "Jiangxi and Hunan, just like that."
At these words, the master was suddenly enlightened. 
The *Wudeng Huiyuan* <note>original: "Record of the Flourishing of the Five Lamps"</note> records: "First visiting Yunmen, the master was asked, 'Where did you just come from?' The master said, 'Chadu.' [Yunmen] asked, 'Where were you during the summer?' The master said, 'Hu...'"

explanation in your presence. I have read in the *History of the Han Dynasty* <note>original: "Han Chuan"</note> how Sima Changqing <note>Sima Xiangru, a famous poet</note> returned to his home in Chengdu to find only four bare walls standing. I have also seen in the Tang Dynasty calligraphy rubbings how Yan Lugong <note>Yan Zhenqing, a noted official and calligrapher</note> begged for rice from Lord Li. Alas! Even figures of the Han and Tang like Changqing and Lugong, who could be called grand, eminent, and heroic, still had broken houses and insufficient gruel. How much more so for those of lesser status! Yet the lingering excellence of these two men’s characters can still be imagined. As for my own unworthiness, my reputation is dull and forgotten, and I have sunk to the bottom. This is because the gap between wisdom and folly cannot be shifted, and the distance between the noble and the lowly is vast; there is no use in envying them. However, I still find something to envy in Changqing and Lugong: I envy that they were alone in their plight. Changqing was indeed weary of travel when he returned, and his only burden was his wife, Wenjun; he still had those "four walls" to boast of. But in my case, I have sought a government salary and not yet attained it, while my parents are now both old and I have no means to support them. My younger brothers and sisters are numerous, reaching the age for marriage—more than twenty mouths in total. All these responsibilities are

<summary>The author compares his own poverty and family burdens to the historical hardships of Sima Xiangru and Yan Zhenqing, noting that his situation is more dire due to his large family.</summary>
<keywords>Sima Xiangru, Yan Zhenqing, poverty, filial piety, Han Dynasty, Tang Dynasty</keywords>

I once visited Ma-ren Temple with Lin Min-gong and Zi-ren. Although it was known for its adherence to the <term>Vinaya</term> <gloss>monastic rules</gloss>, its Chan regulations were no less strict than elsewhere. The granaries had no surplus grain. In the dining hall, Yangshan sighed and said: "This man's spiritual practice will one day reach the Wu and Yue regions. He will only stop when he encounters the 'wind' <note>a reference to a prophecy or a specific location</note>." 

I asked: "Is there anyone who can continue his work?" 

He replied: "To offer this deep heart to the infinite lands is called repaying the Buddha's kindness." 

Thus, the world claims that Nian Fahua is the reincarnation of Yangshan. How can one know that Wen is not the reincarnation of Master Feng? 

Zi-ren said: "He shoulders the Great Dharma and engages in worldly activities here. Are Yangshan and Master Feng of the same rank?"

He was seventy-eight years old and had been a monk for fifty-two years. On the day of his <term>cremation</term> <gloss>ritual burning</gloss>, the flames turned five colors and a white light leaped upward. Wherever the smoke reached, <term>sarira</term> <gloss>sacred relics</gloss> were distributed. Over a thousand people, both monastics and laity, obtained them, and those remaining were beyond counting. A stupa was built for him at the foot of <term>Duxiu Feng</term> <gloss>Solitary Beauty Peak</gloss>. 

The Master was pure, sincere, and compassionate by nature. His refined spirit was extraordinary and elegantly transcendent. He treated everyone, whether strangers or kin, noble or humble, with a warm face and soft words, showing equal respect to all. He presided over the <term>Conglin</term> <gloss>monastic community</gloss> with very strict discipline; those who violated orders were certainly punished without pardon. For this reason, the five seats of the practice centers he held became models for all directions. He attained the <term>Samadhi of Playful Joy</term> and possessed the eloquence of joyful preaching. His sharp wit and wisdom cut down the forest of heterodoxy like falling clouds or collapsing rocks. He opened up the Right View, which shone as clearly as the sun in a blue sky. Everyone felt they had reached the profound depths. However, when entering his room for private instruction, he was like a bronze cliff or an iron wall, impossible to scale.

<summary>The miraculous events of Master Zhenjing's cremation and a description of his dual character: compassionate and polite in person, yet strict in discipline and profound in teaching.</summary>
<keywords>sarira, cremation, Duxiu Feng, Samadhi, Right View, Chan instruction</keywords>

## Volume 30

A commoner from Shuzhou named Ke Meng encountered an extraordinary monk at the foot of Mount Sui. The monk pointed his staff at a pine root and told Meng to carve into it. Meng discovered a "prophetic stone" with a seal script inscription that recognized the "National Destiny of the Sacred Song Dynasty as Boundless." Meng presented the stone at the capital. Emperor Taizong sent an imperial envoy to offer a vegetarian feast at Mount Zhong. He issued a decree that from then on, the Master should not be addressed by his name to show extraordinary respect, and bestowed upon him the title Great Master Daolin Zhenjue <gloss>True Enlightenment of the Path Forest</gloss>.

"Avoid seeking it from others,
For it is far from me.
Now I go alone,
And meet it everywhere.
I am not it now,
Yet it is indeed me.
Only when you understand in this way,
Can you truly attain suchness."

...you do not know that the body is fundamentally the same as emptiness. The body and the shadow are fundamentally no different. Do not have one existence or one non-existence. If you want to keep one and discard the other, you will forever be distant from the true principle. If you further love the sage and hate the ordinary, you will drift and sink in the sea of birth and death. Afflictions exist because of the mind; if there is no mind, where would the afflictions dwell? Do not labor to differentiate or grasp and discard; naturally, you will attain the Dao in an instant. When dreaming, one creates things in the dream; when awake, there is absolutely nothing. The thinking while awake and the dream are inverted; the two views are not different. To change from confusion to awakening and seek profit is no different from a peddling merchant. When movement and stillness are both forgotten, constant silence naturally accords with true suchness. If one says that sentient beings are different from the Buddha, it is far and eternally distinct from the Buddha. The Buddha and sentient beings are not two; it is naturally complete without remainder.

The nature of Dharma is fundamentally always silent, vast, and without boundaries. If the mind grasps between grasping and discarding, it is replaced by that one state. Restrain your appearance, enter <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>meditation</gloss>, sit in Zen, control your environment, and settle your mind. If you carefully examine the mechanism, it is like a wooden person. How can one ever reach the other shore in cultivating the Dao? All phenomena are fundamentally empty, and there is no true attachment.

唯論見性。不論禪定解脫。宗曰。何不論禪定解脫。謂曰。為是二法。不是佛法。佛法是不二之法。宗又問。如何是佛法不二之法。能曰。法師講涅槃經。經明見佛性。是佛法不二之法。如涅槃經高貴德王菩薩白佛言。犯四重禁。作五逆罪。及一闡提等。當斷善根佛性否。佛言。善根有二。一者常。二者無常。佛性非常非無常。是故不斷。名為不二。一者善。二者不善。佛性非善非不善。是名不二。蘊之與界。凡夫見二。智者了達其性無二。無二之性。即是佛性。印宗聞說。歡喜合掌言。某甲講經。猶如瓦礫。仁者論義。猶如真金。於是為能剃髮。願事為師。能遂於菩提樹下開東山法門。能於東山得法。辛苦受盡。命似懸絲。今日得與史君官僚僧尼道俗同此一會。莫非累劫之因。亦是過去生中供養諸佛。同種善根。方始得聞如上頓教得法之因。教是先聖所傳。不是惠能自智。願聞先聖教者。各令淨心。聞了各自除疑。如先世聖人無別。師復告眾曰。善知識。菩提般若之智。世人本自有之。只緣心迷。不能自悟。須假大善知識示導見性。當知愚人智人。佛性本無差別。只緣迷悟不同。所以有愚有智。吾今為說摩訶般若波羅蜜法。使汝等各得智慧。志心諦聽。吾為汝說。善知識。世人終日口念般若。不識自性般若。猶如說食不飽。口但說空。萬劫不得見性。終無有益。善知識。摩訶般若波羅蜜是梵語。此言大智慧到彼岸。此須心行。不在口念。口念心不行。

We only discuss seeing one's true nature <note>original: "見性", the core realization in Zen</note>. We do not discuss meditative concentration <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> or liberation. 

Yinzong asked: Why do you not discuss meditative concentration and liberation? 

Huineng replied: Because these are two separate things, and thus not the Buddha-Dharma. The Buddha-Dharma is a teaching of non-duality <note>original: "不二之法", the principle that reality is not composed of opposing pairs</note>. 

Yinzong asked again: What is this Buddha-Dharma of non-duality? 

Huineng said: Master, you lecture on the Nirvana Sutra. This sutra clarifies that seeing the Buddha-nature is the Buddha-Dharma of non-duality. As the Nirvana Sutra states, the Bodhisattva Noble Virtue King asked the Buddha: If someone commits the four gravest sins, the five heinous crimes, or is an <term>icchantika</term> <gloss>one who lacks the seeds of enlightenment</gloss>, do they cut off their roots of goodness and their Buddha-nature? 

The Buddha replied: There are two kinds of roots of goodness. The first is permanent, and the second is impermanent. However, the Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent. Therefore, it is never cut off. This is called non-duality. Furthermore, there is good and there is not-good. The Buddha-nature is neither good nor not-good. This is called non-duality. Ordinary people see the physical aggregates and the sensory realms as two separate things. The wise realize that their nature is not two. This nature of non-duality is the Buddha-nature.

Upon hearing this, Yinzong rejoiced and joined his palms in reverence. He said: My lecturing on the sutras is like common rubble, while your discussion of the meaning is like pure gold. 

Thereupon, he shaved Huineng’s head and requested to serve him as a disciple. Huineng then opened the Dharma Gate of the East Mountain <note>the lineage of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren</note> under a Bodhi tree. 

Huineng continued: I received the Dharma at East Mountain and endured extreme hardships. My life hung by a thread. That I am able to meet with the Prefect, the officials, monks, nuns, and laypeople in this assembly today is due to causes from many kalpas <gloss>eons</gloss> ago. It is also because you made offerings to many Buddhas in past lives and planted shared roots of goodness that you are now able to hear this sudden teaching <note>original: "頓教", the doctrine of immediate enlightenment</note> and the causes of my receiving the Dharma. This teaching was passed down by the ancient sages; it is not my own personal wisdom. Those who wish to hear the teaching of the ancient sages should each purify their minds. After hearing it, each of you will resolve your own doubts, becoming no different from the sages of past generations.

The Master then addressed the assembly: Good friends, the wisdom of <term>Bodhi-Prajna</term> <gloss>enlightened wisdom</gloss> is something people of this world inherently possess. It is only because the mind is deluded that they cannot realize it themselves. They must rely on a great spiritual friend to show them the way and guide them to see their nature. You should know that there is no difference in the Buddha-nature of an ignorant person and a wise person. It is only because of the difference between delusion and awakening that some are ignorant and some are wise. I shall now speak to you of the Great <term>Prajna Paramita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> so that each of you may attain wisdom. Listen carefully with a sincere heart, and I will speak for you.

Good friends, people of the world recite <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss> with their mouths all day long, but they do not recognize the <term>Prajna</term> of their own nature. This is like talking about food but never becoming full. If you only speak of emptiness with your mouth, you will not see your nature even after ten thousand kalpas. In the end, there is no benefit. 

Good friends, <term>Maha Prajna Paramita</term> is a Sanskrit term. In our language, it means "Great Wisdom that reaches the Other Shore." This must be practiced in the heart; it does not consist of oral recitation. If the mouth recites it but the heart does not practice it, it is of no use.

<summary>Huineng explains the principle of non-duality through the Nirvana Sutra and begins his public teaching on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, emphasizing internal practice over mere recitation.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Yinzong, non-duality, Buddha-nature, Nirvana Sutra, Prajna Paramita, sudden teaching, East Mountain Dharma Gate</keywords>

多。迷人不能省覺。念念起惡。常行惡道。迴一念善。智慧即生。此名自性化身佛。何名圓滿報身。譬如一燈能除千年暗。一智能滅萬年愚。莫思向前。已過不可得。常思於後。念念圓明。自見本性。善惡雖殊。本性無二。無二之性。名為實性。於實性中。不染善惡。此名圓滿報身。自性起一念惡。滅萬劫善因。自性起一念善。得恆沙惡盡。直至無上菩提。念念自見。不失本念。名為報身。善知識。從法身思量。即是化身佛。念念自性自見。即是報身佛。自悟自修自性功德。是真歸依。皮肉是色身。色身是舍宅。不言歸依也。但悟自性三身。即識自性佛。吾有一無相頌。若能誦持。言下令汝積劫迷罪一時消滅。頌曰。迷人修福不修道。只言修福便是道。布施供養福無邊。心中三惡元來造。擬將修福欲滅罪。後世得福罪還在。但向心中除罪緣。各自性中真懺悔。忽悟大乘真懺悔。除邪行正即無罪。學道常於自性觀。即與諸佛同一類。吾祖惟傳此頓法。普願見性同一體。若欲當來覓法身。離諸法相心中洗。努力自見莫悠悠。後念忽絕一世休。若悟大乘得見性。虔恭合掌至心求。師言。善知識。總須誦取。依此修行。言下見性。雖去吾千里。如常在吾邊。於此言下不悟。即對面千里。何勤遠來。珍重好去。一眾聞法。靡不開悟。歡喜奉行。

There are many such people. Deluded people cannot awaken themselves. Their every thought gives rise to evil, and they constantly walk the paths of evil. Yet, if they turn back a single thought toward goodness, wisdom is immediately born. This is called the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Transformation Body</gloss> of one's own nature.

What is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Reward Body</gloss>? Just as a single lamp can dispel a thousand years of darkness, a single flash of wisdom can extinguish ten thousand years of ignorance. Do not dwell on what came before; the past is gone and cannot be recovered. Always think of what comes after. Let every thought be perfect and bright, and you will see your own original nature. Although good and evil differ, the original nature is not two. This non-dual nature is called the true nature. Within this true nature, one is not stained by either good or evil. This is called the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Reward Body</gloss>.

If a single evil thought arises from one's own nature, it destroys the good causes of ten thousand <term>kalpas</term> <gloss>aeons</gloss>. If a single good thought arises from one's own nature, it ends evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, leading directly to supreme <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>Enlightenment</gloss>. To see for oneself in every thought and never lose the original thought is called the Reward Body.

Learned friends, to deliberate from the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> is the Transformation Body Buddha. When every thought sees into its own nature, that is the Reward Body Buddha. To realize and cultivate the merit of one's own nature for oneself is the true refuge. The skin and flesh are the physical body; the physical body is merely a house and is not spoken of as a refuge. Simply realize the three bodies of your own nature, and you will recognize the Buddha of your own nature.

I have a Verse of Formlessness. If you can recite and maintain it, it will cause the deluded sins accumulated over many aeons to vanish the moment the words are spoken. The verse says:

Deluded people cultivate blessings but not the Way,
Claiming that cultivating blessings is the Way itself.
While the blessings from charity and offerings are limitless,
The three evils remain rooted in the mind.
By attempting to use the cultivation of blessings to wipe out sins,
One receives blessings in future lives, but the sins remain.
One must simply remove the conditions of sin from within the mind,
And practice true repentance within one's own nature.
A sudden realization of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> true repentance,
Removing the false and practicing the right, leaves one without sin.
Those who study the Way should constantly observe their own nature;
They are then of the same kind as all Buddhas.
Our ancestors transmitted only this sudden teaching,
Wishing that all might see their nature and become one substance.
If you wish to seek the Truth Body in the future,
Leave all appearances of phenomena and wash your heart within.
Strive to see it for yourself; do not drift aimlessly.
If the next thought is suddenly cut off, this life is over.
If you realize the Great Vehicle and see your nature,
Join your palms in reverence and seek it with a sincere heart.

The Master said: Learned friends, you must all recite this and practice according to it. If you see your nature upon hearing these words, then even if you are a thousand miles from me, it will be as if you are always by my side. If you do not realize it upon hearing these words, then even if we are face to face, we are a thousand miles apart. Why bother coming from so far? Take care and go well.

The entire assembly heard the Dharma, and there were none who did not achieve awakening. They rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

<summary>The Sixth Patriarch explains the Reward Body of Buddha and provides the Verse of Formlessness to guide practitioners in seeing their true nature rather than merely seeking external blessings. He emphasizes that true repentance and sudden enlightenment come from within the mind.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Platform Sutra, Reward Body, Transformation Body, Verse of Formlessness, Repentance, Buddha-nature, Sudden Enlightenment</keywords>

人。通達無取捨。以知五蘊法。及以蘊中我。外現眾色像。一一音聲相。平等如夢幻。不起凡聖見。不作涅槃解。二邊三際斷。常應諸根用。而不起用想。分別一切法。不起分別想。劫火燒海底。風鼓山相擊。真常寂滅樂。涅槃相如是。吾今強言說。令汝捨邪見。汝勿隨言解。許汝知少分。志道聞偈大悟。踴躍作禮而退。行思禪師。姓劉氏。吉州安城人也。聞曹溪法席盛化。徑來參禮。遂問曰。當何所務。即不落階級。師曰。汝曾作甚麼來。曰。聖諦亦不為。師曰。落何階級。曰。聖諦尚不為。何階級之有。師深器之。令思首眾。一日。師謂曰。汝當分化一方。無令斷絕。思既得法。遂回吉州青原山。弘法紹化。諡號弘濟禪師。懷讓禪師。金州杜氏子也。初謁嵩山安國師。安發之曹溪參扣。讓至。禮拜。師曰。甚處來。曰。嵩山。師曰。甚麼物恁麼來。曰。說似一物即不中。師曰。還可修證否。曰。修證即不無。污染即不得。師曰。只此不污染。諸佛之所護念。汝既如是。吾亦如是。西天般若多羅讖。汝足下出一馬駒。踏殺天下人。應在汝心。不須速說。讓豁然契會。遂執侍左右十五載。日益玄奧。後往南嶽。大闡禪宗。永嘉玄覺禪師。少習經論。精天台止觀法門。因看維摩經。發明心地。偶師弟子玄策相訪。與其劇談。出言暗合諸祖。策云。仁者得法師誰。曰。我聽方等經論。各有師承。後於維摩經悟佛心宗。未有證明者。策云。威音王已前即得。

A person who is thoroughly realized has no sense of grasping or rejecting. By knowing the <term>five skandhas</term> <gloss>the five aggregates of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness</gloss> and the self within those aggregates, they see that all external forms and every sound are equal, like a dream or an illusion. They do not give rise to views of "ordinary" or "holy," nor do they form intellectual interpretations of <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state of liberation from suffering and rebirth</gloss>. The two extremes <note>such as existence and non-existence</note> and the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note> are cut off. They constantly respond to the functions of the sensory organs, yet they do not give rise to the thought of "functioning." They distinguish all phenomena, yet do not give rise to the thought of "distinction." Even when the fires at the end of an eon burn the seabed, or the winds lash the mountains against one another, the joy of true, eternal, and peaceful extinction remains. Such is the nature of Nirvana. I now speak of it under constraint to make you abandon false views. Do not follow my words with literal interpretations, and I will allow that you have understood a small portion. Zhidao heard this verse and attained great awakening. Overjoyed, he bowed and withdrew.

Zen Master Xingsi was born to the Liu family in Ancheng, Jizhou. Hearing that the Dharma seat at Caoxi was flourishing, he went directly to pay his respects. He asked, "What must one do so as not to fall into stages or ranks?" The Master <note>Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch</note> asked, "What have you been doing?" Xingsi replied, "I do not even practice the Holy Truths." The Master asked, "Then what stage have you fallen into?" Xingsi replied, "If I do not even practice the Holy Truths, what stage could there be?" The Master deeply appreciated his capacity and made Xingsi the leader of the assembly. One day, the Master told him, "You should go and teach in your own region so that the lineage is not cut off." Having received the Dharma, Xingsi returned to Mount Qingyuan in Jizhou to spread the teachings. He was posthumously titled Zen Master Hongji.

Zen Master Huairang was the son of the Du family in Jinzhou. He first visited National Teacher Anguo at Mount Song. Anguo sent him to Caoxi to consult the Master. When Huairang arrived and bowed, the Master asked, "Where do you come from?" Huairang replied, "From Mount Song." The Master asked, "What is this thing that has come here?" Huairang replied, "To say it is like a thing would be off the mark." The Master asked, "Can it still be cultivated and realized?" Huairang replied, "It is not that there is no cultivation or realization, but it cannot be defiled." The Master said, "Just this 'not being defiled' is what all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. You are like this, and I am like this too. Prajnatara of India predicted that a young horse would emerge from under your feet and trample the people of the world. This will happen in your heart; there is no need to speak of it quickly." Huairang suddenly understood. He served the Master for fifteen years, growing deeper in the profound mysteries every day. Later, he went to Nanyue and greatly promoted the Zen school.

Zen Master Xuanjue of Yongjia studied the sutras and commentaries in his youth and was an expert in the Tiantai school's <term>Samatha-Vipasyana</term> <gloss>calm abiding and insight</gloss> methods. While reading the Vimalakirti Sutra, he realized the ground of his mind. By chance, the Master's disciple Xuance visited him and had a deep discussion. Xuanjue's words were in secret agreement with the Patriarchs. Xuance asked, "Who was your teacher when you attained the Dharma?" Xuanjue said, "I listened to the <term>Vaipulya</term> <gloss>extensive or Mahayana</gloss> sutras and commentaries, and each had a teacher. Later, I realized the Buddha-mind school through the Vimalakirti Sutra, but I have no one to verify it." Xuance said, "Before the time of the King of Awesome Sound <note>the first Buddha of the remote past</note>, that would have been fine."

<summary>This page records the Sixth Patriarch Huineng's instructions on the nature of Nirvana and his initial encounters with three major disciples: Xingsi, Huairang, and Xuanjue. These meetings emphasize direct realization over intellectual study and formal stages of practice.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Xingsi, Huairang, Xuanjue, Nirvana, Vimalakirti Sutra, Zen lineage, Mount Qingyuan, Nanyue, Caoxi</keywords>

And thus they are established. All things are the original mind producing ten thousand kinds of phenomena. Therefore, the sutra says: when the mind arises, various phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease. If you wish to achieve the <term>All-Knowledge</term> <gloss>the wisdom of a Buddha</gloss>, you must attain the <term>Samadhi of One Appearance</term> <gloss>a state of meditative concentration on the non-duality of all things</gloss> and the <term>Samadhi of One Practice</term> <gloss>the constant practice of maintaining a straightforward mind</gloss>. If, in all places, you do not cling to appearances, and within those appearances you do not give rise to resentment or love, nor have any grasping or rejection, and do not dwell on matters of profit, loss, or destruction, but remain peaceful, quiet, empty, harmonious, and indifferent, this is called the Samadhi of One Appearance. If, in all places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you maintain a pure and straightforward mind, without moving from the <term>Bodhimaṇḍa</term> <gloss>place of enlightenment</gloss>, truly becoming the Pure Land, this is called the Samadhi of One Practice. If a person possesses these two samadhis, it is like the earth having seeds: they are contained, nourished, and their fruits are matured. The Samadhi of One Appearance and One Practice are just like this. My current teaching of the Law is like a timely rain, universally moistening the great earth. Your Buddha-nature is like the seeds; meeting this moisture, they all begin to grow. Those who receive my instructions will certainly attain <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>. Those who follow my practice will surely realize the wonderful fruit. Listen to my verse:

The mind-ground contains all seeds,
Under the universal rain, all sprout.
Once the flower of sudden enlightenment is realized,
The fruit of Bodhi naturally matures.

After the Master spoke the verse, he said: The Law is not dual, and the mind is the same. The Way is pure and without any appearances. You must be careful not to contemplate stillness or empty your minds. This mind is originally pure; there is nothing to grasp or reject. Each of you must exert yourselves and go well according to circumstances. At that time, the disciples bowed and withdrew.

On the eighth day of the seventh month, the Grand Master suddenly said to his followers: I wish to return to Xinzhou. You must quickly prepare the boats and oars. The assembly pleaded with him to stay with great sincerity. The Master said: Even when Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the passing away of a Buddha</gloss>. Whatever comes must go; this is a constant principle. This physical body of mine must have a place to return to. The assembly asked: After the Master leaves this time, when will you return? The Master said: Fallen leaves return to their roots; when I came, I had no mouth <note>This is a Zen metaphor suggesting that the ultimate truth cannot be spoken, or that his return is beyond words</note>.

They asked again: To whom has the <term>Treasury of the True Dharma Eye</term> <gloss>the core essence of the Buddha's teaching</gloss> been transmitted? The Master said: Those who have the Way obtain it; those who are without mind understand it. They asked further: Will there be any difficulties in the future? The Master said: Five or six years after my passing, a person will come to take my head. Listen to my prophecy:

To support the parents upon the head,
There must be food in the mouth.
Encountering the difficulty of Man,
Yang and Liu will be the officials. <note>This cryptic prophecy refers to a historical attempt to steal the Sixth Patriarch's head by a monk hired by a rival school, involving officials named Yang and Liu</note>

He also said: Seventy years after my departure, two <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>enlightened beings</gloss> will come from the East, one a monk and one a layman. They will spread the teachings at the same time, establishing my school, repairing the <term>Sangharamas</term> <gloss>monasteries</gloss>, and making the lineage flourish.

They asked: We do not know how many generations have passed since the ancient Buddhas and Patriarchs first appeared. We pray you will provide an explanation. The Master said: The ancient Buddhas who responded to the world are already beyond count.

<summary>The Sixth Patriarch Huineng explains the Samadhis of One Appearance and One Practice, delivers a final verse on enlightenment, and prepares for his death and return to Xinzhou while prophesying future events of the Zen lineage.</summary>
<keywords>Huineng, Samadhi, Buddha-nature, Bodhi, Nirvana, Xinzhou, Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, prophecy, Zen lineage</keywords>
